tasks.title: Magnetic Field Modeling: T96 model
tasks.description:
Using pySPEDAS, load THEMIS state data for probe A, 2023-03-24, in GSM coordinates. Then download T96 model parameters from OMNI and the Kyoto WDC. Then generate the expected field using the T96 model at the THEMIS-A times and GSM positions, using the downloaded model parameters.

Use this helper function:
from pyspedas.geopack import get_tsy_params
from pytplot import time_double

def get_params(trange, position_var):
    support_trange = [time_double(trange[0])-60*60*24,
                      time_double(trange[1])+60*60*24]
    pyspedas.kyoto.dst(trange=support_trange)
    pyspedas.omni.data(trange=support_trange)
    join_vec(['BX_GSE', 'BY_GSM', 'BZ_GSM'])
    parmod = get_tsy_params('kyoto_dst',
                            'BX_GSE-BY_GSM-BZ_GSM_joined',
                            'proton_density',
                            'flow_speed',
                            model='t96',
                            pressure_tvar='Pressure',
                            g_variables=None,
                            speed=True)
    pyspedas.tinterpol(parmod,position_var,newname='parmod_interpolated')
    return 'parmod_interpolated'
tasks.hint: pyspedas.themis.state(), varnames="tha_pos_gsm"; from pyspedas.geopack import tt96; tt96(position_variable,params); position variable + "_bt96"

tasks.title: Interpolating Time
tasks.description:
For analysis, it's often useful to align two datasets with different timestamps onto the same time grid. This can be done by various methods such as:
  • Converting HAPI timestamps to datetime objects and then to integers for interpolation, and using functions from NumPy or SciPy for interpolation. Datetime conversion methods can also be employed here.
  • Using a Pandas DataFrame's interpolation methods after placing the data within it.
  • Employing the 'interpol' function from 'spacepy.toolbox' as demonstrated in the SpacePy tutorial.
Begin with a script that reads datasets from two different servers. Perform the following steps:
  1. Interpolate 'data2' onto the time grid of 'data0'.
  2. Create a table or plot for a visual comparison of interpolated and original values.
  3. Average 'data0' into 1-hour bins and compare with 'data2'.
The initial program:
from hapiclient import hapi, hapitime2datetime

server     = 'https://cdaweb.gsfc.nasa.gov/hapi'
dataset    = 'AC_H0_SWE'
parameters = 'Np'
start      = '1998-02-04'
stop       = '1998-02-06'

data0, meta0 = hapi(server, dataset, parameters, start, stop)
print('data0 = ')
print(data0)

server     = 'https://cdaweb.gsfc.nasa.gov/hapi'
dataset    = 'AC_H2_SWE'
parameters = 'Np'
start      = '1998-02-04'
stop       = '1998-02-06'

data2, meta2 = hapi(server, dataset, parameters, start, stop)
print('\ndata2 = ')
print(data2)

tasks.title: Comparing Perspectives: Reproject SDO AIA and STEREO EUVI Solar Images
tasks.description:
As solar phenomena are often studied from multiple viewpoints to gain a three-dimensional understanding, your task is to use SunPy and the reproject package to fetch and plot images of the sun from both SDO AIA and STEREO EUVI, showing the solar limb from both perspectives on both images, and to reproject their views. Do the following:
  1. Download an image of the sun in the 193 Ångstrom wavelength from SDO AIA at the timestamp 2012-06-01/00:00:07.
  2. Download an image of the sun in the 195 Ångstrom wavelength from STEREO EUVI at the timestamp 2012-06-01/00:05:30.
  3. Resample the images to 512x512 pixels to reduce memory consumption.
  4. Plot them side by side, highlighting the solar limb as seen by both instruments in each.
  5. Use the reproject library to reproject the EUVI image to the viewpoint of the AIA.
  6. And vice versa, reproject the AIA image to the viewpoint of the EUVI (effectively showing how each spacecraft would see the sun's region covered by the other).
  7. Plot the reprojected images side by side for comparison.
tasks.hint: Use SunPy's Fido interface to fetch the images, and the reproject_to() method to reproject one image to the other's perspective. Draw the solar limb in each plot for both the original and reprojected images to visualize the changes in perspective. To ensure the perspectives align correctly, you may need to adjust the metadata of one image to match the other's reference solar radius (rsun_ref) before reprojection. Images as seen from the other's perspective will appear as partial slices of the sphere that is the sun.

tasks.title: Compute OMNI Plasma Beta with PlasmaPy
tasks.description: Using the HAPI client, download the following OMNI data from CDAWeb for 2003-09-01T00:00:00Z to 2003-09-02T00:00:00Z: ABS_B1800, T1800, N1800, and Beta1800. Convert the magnetic field, proton temperature, and proton density arrays into Astropy quantities, use PlasmaPy's `beta()` to calculate plasma beta at each timestamp, then plot your PlasmaPy beta time series together with the OMNI Beta1800 time series. The two curves will not line up — explain why.
tasks.hint: Use `hapi()`, `hapitime2datetime()`, and PlasmaPy's `beta()`. The HAPI metadata contains parameter units and fill values. Compare PlasmaPy's single-species formula `n*k_B*T / (B^2 / (2*mu_0))` with OMNI's definition `[(T*4.16e-5) + 5.34] * Np / B^2`. PlasmaPy's `beta()` only accounts for proton thermal pressure, while OMNI's `Beta1800` adds a fixed electron contribution — so expect the PlasmaPy series to sit below OMNI's.

tasks.title: Tracking MMS from Bear Mountain
tasks.description: Using the MMS MEC file, create a `Coords` object for MMS position from `2020-10-11 00:00` to `04:00` UTC, convert it to an Astropy `SkyCoord`, transform it to `AltAz` for Bear Mountain (`41.3 deg N`, `74.0 deg W`, `390 m`), and plot MMS altitude versus time. Report the UTC time and altitude of maximum elevation.
tasks.hint: Use `Coords.to_skycoord()`, `Ticktock.APT`, `astropy.coordinates.EarthLocation`, and `AltAz`.

tasks.title: Summarize ICON IVM by Orbit
tasks.description: Using pysat, instantiate the ICON IVM instrument with `orbit_info={'kind':'lt','index':'Magnetic_Local_Time'}`, load data for 2020-01-03, attach a custom function that adds a log ion density variable, and produce per-orbit panel plots for the first five orbits.
tasks.hint: Register ICON IVM with `pysat.utils.registry.register(['pysatNASA.instruments.icon_ivm'])`, instantiate `pysat.Instrument('icon','ivm',inst_id='a', orbit_info=orbit_info)`, use `inst.custom_attach(...)` to add the log-density variable, and iterate via `for orbit in inst.orbits:`.

tasks.title: Bin ICON IVM with pysatSeasons
tasks.description: Using pysat, register ICON IVM, instantiate `pysat.Instrument('icon','ivm',inst_id='a')`, and set bounds from 2020-01-01 to 2020-01-05. Attach a custom function that creates `Log_Ion_Density = np.log10(inst['Ion_Density'])`, compute 2D medians of `Ion_Temperature` and `Log_Ion_Density` over an MLT axis of `[0, 24, 24]` and a longitude axis of `[0, 360, 30]` using `pysatSeasons.avg.median2D`, and plot both 2D distributions.
tasks.hint: Use `pysat.utils.registry.register(['pysatNASA.instruments.icon_ivm'])`, `inst.custom_attach(add_log_dens)`, and `pysatSeasons.avg.median2D(inst, [0,24,24], 'Magnetic_Local_Time', [0,360,30], 'Longitude', ['Ion_Temperature','Log_Ion_Density'], return_data=True)`.

tasks.title: Make a LASCO Running-Difference Movie
tasks.description: Using SunPy, fetch SOHO/LASCO C2 images from 2023-03-20T13:00 to 2023-03-20T19:00. Load them as a Map sequence, exposure-normalize each frame, build a running-difference sequence by subtracting adjacent frames, and animate the result.
tasks.hint: Use `Fido` with `a.Instrument.lasco` and `a.Detector('C2')`, then `sunpy.map.Map(..., sequence=True)`. Normalize each frame by its `EXPTIME`, build adjacent difference frames, and animate with matplotlib.

tasks.title: Overlay HEK Flare Locations
tasks.description: Using SunPy's Fido and HEK client, query HEK for solar flares with GOES class greater than C2.5 between 2022-03-28T11:00 and 2022-03-28T14:00. Build helioprojective coordinates from the event metadata and overlay the flare locations on co-temporal SDO AIA and STEREO/SECCHI 304 Å maps.
tasks.hint: Search HEK with `a.hek.FL` plus a GOES class threshold, build `Helioprojective` coordinates from the event metadata, and use `ax.plot_coord(...)` to overlay on each map.

tasks.title: Model Epoch-Dependent Cutoff Rigidity
tasks.description: Using SpacePy, compute Störmer cutoff rigidity at epochs from 1900-01-01 to 2025-01-01 in 90-day steps, for L shells of 2, 3, 4, and 5, using IGRF dipole moments. Plot cutoff rigidity versus epoch with one line per L shell, and add a secondary y-axis showing the equivalent proton energy.
tasks.hint: Follow the workflow in `SpacePy - Cutoff Rigidities.md`. Iterate over epochs and L shells, and use matplotlib `twinx` for the proton-energy axis.

tasks.title: Compare SWMF North/South IMF Runs
tasks.description: Open the northward and southward IMF SWMF tutorial outputs from `swmf_ssi_north` and `swmf_ssi_south`. For each case, load `GM/y=0_mhd_1_e20150321-060040-000_20150321-060510-000.outs` with `pybats.bats.Bats2d`, the matching `IE/it{time}_000.idl.gz` files with `pybats.rim.Iono`, and `GM/log_e20150321-054500.log` with `pybats.LogFile`. Compare pressure and FAC panels and Dst traces between the two IMF cases.
tasks.hint: Use `spacepy.pybats.bats.Bats2d`, `spacepy.pybats.rim.Iono`, and `spacepy.pybats.LogFile`. Iterate IE files using each MHD frame's timestamp formatted as `IE/it{t_now:%y%m%d_%H%M%S}_000.idl.gz`.

tasks.title: Summarize Ionization States
tasks.description: Using PlasmaPy, create `IonizationState` objects for `He-4` with ionic fractions `[0.1, 0.7, 0.2]` and for `C` with ionic fractions `[0, 0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.30, 0.15, 0.05]`, both at total number density `1e7 cm^-3`. For each element, report the electron density `n_e`, the mean charge `Z_mean`, and the average ion.
tasks.hint: Use `plasmapy.particles.IonizationState`. Read `.n_e` for electron density and `.Z_mean` for mean charge, and use `.average_ion()` for the average ion.

tasks.title: Find Beta-Equals-One Field Strength
tasks.description: For coronal plasma with `T = 1 MK` and `n = 1e9 cm^-3`, sweep magnetic field strength from `1 G` to `100 G` in log-spaced steps using PlasmaPy's `beta()`. Plot beta versus B on a log-log axis and report the B value where beta is closest to 1.
tasks.hint: Use `numpy.logspace(0, 2, ...) * u.G`, then `plasmapy.formulary.beta(T, n, B)` with the array B. Plot with matplotlib `loglog` and use `np.argmin(np.abs(beta - 1))`.
